title: BVA Decision 25000005: Special monthly compensation based on the need for aid and attendance is granted, subject to the rules and regulations governing the payment of VA monetary benefits
text:
Citation Nr: 25000005
Decision Date: 01/02/25	Archive Date: 01/02/25

DOCKET NO. 16-49 436
DATE: January 2, 2025

ORDER

Special monthly compensation based on the need for aid and attendance is granted, subject to the rules and regulations governing the payment of VA monetary benefits.

FINDING OF FACT

The Veteran is shown to be in need of regular aid and attendance by reason of service-connected disability.  

CONCLUSION OF LAW

The criteria for special monthly compensation based on the need for regular aid and attendance of another person are met.  38 U.S.C. §§ 1114, 1502, 5107; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.102, 3.350, 3.352.  

REASONS AND BASES FOR FINDING AND CONCLUSION

The Veteran had active-duty service from February 1967 to February 1971, to include service in the Republic of Vietnam.  

In July 2016, the RO denied a claim for SMC based on the need for aid and attendance.  

In March 2019, the Veteran was afforded a hearing before the undersigned.  

In April 2020, the Board denied the claim.  The Veteran appealed the decision to the United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims (Court).  In January 2021, the Court granted a Joint Motion for Remand (JMR).  In October 2022, the Board denied the claim a second time.  In July 2023, the Court granted a JMR.

The Board remanded the claim in March 2022 and January 2024.

In December 2024, a waiver of AOJ review was received.  Accordingly, a remand for AOJ review is not required.  38 C.F.R. § 20.1304 (c).  

1.  Special monthly compensation (SMC).

In November 2010, the RO granted special monthly pension based on the need for aid and attendance.  

In May 2011, the RO determined that the Veteran is not competent to handle disbursement of VA funds.  

In February 2016, the Veteran filed a claim for SMC.  See Veteran's VA Form 21-526EZ and VA Form 21-2680, received in February 2016.  In July 2016, the RO denied the claim.  The Veteran has appealed.  

Service connection is currently in effect for PTSD to include anxiety and depression, evaluated as 100 percent disabling effective June 8, 2010.     

The anatomical loss or loss of use of both feet, one hand and one foot, or loss of vision in both eyes, or is permanently bedridden or with such significant disabilities as to be in need or require the regular aid and attendance of another person under the criteria set forth in 38 C.F.R. § 3.352(a).  38 U.S.C. § 1114(l); 38 C.F.R. § 3.350 (b)(3).  

When determining whether the regular aid and attendance of another person is needed, the following factors are considered: inability to dress or undress oneself, or to keep oneself ordinarily clean and presentable; frequent need of adjustment of any special prosthetic or orthopedic appliances which by reason of the particular disability cannot be done without such aid; inability to feed oneself through the loss of coordination of upper extremities or through extreme weakness; inability to attend to the wants of nature; or an incapacity, physical or mental, which requires care or assistance on a regular basis to protect the Veteran from the hazards or dangers incident to his or her daily environment.  38 C.F.R. § 3.352 (a).

For the purposes of 38 C.F.R. § 3.352 (a), "bedridden" is a proper basis for determining whether the veteran needs regular aid and attendance of another person.  "Bedridden" means that the veteran is actually required to remain in bed.  38 C.F.R. §§ 3.350 (b)(4), 3.352(a).  Voluntarily taking to bed or being prescribed bed rest for the greater or lesser part of the day to promote convalescence or cure is insufficient.  Determinations that the veteran is so helpless as to be in need of regular aid and attendance will not be based solely upon an opinion that the veteran's condition is such as would require them to be in bed but must be based on the actual requirement of personal assistance from others.  38 C.F.R. § 3.352 (a).

A veteran does not need to demonstrate all the above factors to be found entitled to aid and attendance benefits, and the need for regular aid and attendance does not have to be constant.  The Veteran does not have the loss or loss of use of the feet or hands or vision deficits.  The particular personal functions that the veteran is unable to perform should be considered in connection with their condition as a whole.  38 C.F.R. § 3.352 (a); see also Turco v. Brown, 9 Vet. App. 222, 224 (1996).  

The January 2021 JMR shows that it was agreed that although a July 2019 VA examiner noted the Veteran's PTSD and addressed his condition, the examiner did not discuss what role the Veteran's stroke played in his cognitive and physical impairment.  As a result, it remains unclear as to how much of the Veteran's need for aid and attendance can be attributed to his service-connected PTSD, or his non-service-connected residuals of a stroke.  

In June 2022, another medical opinion was obtained.  In October 2022, the Board denied the claim.  

The July 2023 JMR shows that it was agreed that the Board's October 2022 decision failed to ensure substantial compliance with the January 2021 JMR, which ordered VA to schedule the Veteran for an aid and attendance/housebound examination to determine if his service-connected PTSD alone resulted in physical and/or mental impairments that  rendered him so helpless as to require the regular aid and attendance of another person or result in his being confined to his house.  The JMR stated that in answering that question, the examiner should address the role that the Veteran's non-service-connected stroke residuals played in his cognitive and physical impairment, and the Veteran's spouse's contention that his PTSD symptoms had intensified after the stroke.  The JMR states that the June 2022 examiner appears to have limited her opinion to whether the Veteran still suffered from PTSD.  

A statement from the Veteran's spouse, received in February 2016, shows that he reports the following: The Veteran had a stroke five years ago, leaving him with paralysis to the right side of his body and speech impairment.  He is house bound.  He needs daily assistance with bathing, feeding, dressing, attending to the wants of nature, and protection from household hazards.   

By way of history, a VA examination for housebound status or permanent need for regular aid and attendance report (VA Form 21-2680) dated in June 2010 showed that the diagnosis was left MCA (middle cerebral artery) stroke with right hemiparesis and fluent and near-fluent aphasia.  This report indicated that the Veteran requires nursing home care due to right hemiparesis.  He cannot feed himself or prepare his own meals.  He requires medication management due to aphasia.  He cannot manage his own financial affairs.  He had 0/5 strength in his right upper extremity, and 5/5 strength in his left upper extremity.  Strength in the bilateral lower extremities was 2/5.  He is generally bed-bound.  Other VA reports dated in 2010 showed that the Veteran was in rehabilitation following a stroke in April 2010.  The findings included cognitive impairment and aphasia.  There was a notation that the Veteran was suffering from an adjustment disorder with anxiety and depression secondary to his stroke.  See October 2010 VA PTSD examination report.  

In July 2012, the RO increased the Veteran's rating for PTSD to 100 percent, citing symptoms that included anxiety, chronic sleep impairment, and depressed mood.  

The evidence dated during the time period in issue includes a May 2016 VA examination for housebound status or permanent need for regular aid and attendance report (VA Form 21-2680) which indicates the following: The Veteran is able to feed himself, but only with his left upper extremity; he cannot use his right upper extremity.  He cannot speak.  He is confined to bed around the clock.  He cannot prepare his own meals.  He is not legally blind and does not require nursing home care.  He requires medication management.  He cannot manage his own financial affairs.  He is wheelchair bound.  He weight-bears with assistance.  He has poor balance.  He cannot leave his home without assistance.  He needs assistance with bathing and tending to other hygiene needs.   

VA progress notes include notations that the Veteran's yes and no responses were inconsistent and incorrect when asked fairly simple questions, suggesting prominent semantic language impairments.  Sentence length was markedly reduced, only 1 or 2 words at a time, and he was unable to follow simple commands.  The diagnoses included cognitive disorder NOS (not otherwise specified).  Follow-up psychiatric care was recommended to monitor his mood and response to antidepressant medications.  The Veteran's medications included venlafaxine for PTSD and depression, which was increased (doubled) in October 2015.  

A July 2019 VA examination for housebound status or permanent need for regular aid and attendance report (VA Form 21-2680) shows the following: The Veteran is not legally blind and does not require nursing home care.  He requires medication management.  He is able to feed himself, but he cannot prepare his own meals.  He needs assistance in bathing and tending to other hygiene needs.  He cannot manage his own benefits payments or to direct someone to do so.  On examination, he was in a wheelchair.  He could not speak or use his right upper extremity.  He needs help with dressing, transfers, and toileting.  He cannot use his right lower extremity well.  He can only stand or leave his home with assistance, and he requires a wheelchair to leave his home.  He has poor cognitive function.  The diagnosis was PTSD.  

A June 2022 VA PTSD DBQ shows that the Veteran's symptoms were noted to include crying spells, anxiety, sleep difficulties, and difficulty in understanding complex commands.  Speech was unable to be assessed, as he only said "no."  Judgment, insight, thought process, and orientation were unable to be assessed.  The diagnosis was PTSD.  

A June 2022 VA examination for housebound status or permanent need for regular aid and attendance report (VA Form 21-2680) includes findings that the Veteran can feed himself.  He has poor balance, and he occasionally chokes.  He cannot prepare his own meals.  He requires assistance for dressing and undressing.  He requires assistance for bathing, grooming, shaving, and toileting.  The diagnosis was status post infarct with right-sided paralysis.  

A June 2022 VA medical opinion from a psychologist shows that the examiner concluded that the Veteran's service-connected PTSD alone is less likely than not results in physical and/or mental impairments that render him so helpless as to require the regular aid and attendance of another person or result in his being confined to his house.  

A February 2024 VA medical opinion shows that the examiner concluded, "It is my opinion that the claimant's service-connected PTSD alone results in physical and/or mental impairments is less than likely than not render him so helpless as to require the regular aid and attendance of another person or result in his generally being confined to his house."    

The Board finds that the criteria for special monthly compensation based on the need for aid and attendance have been met.  The May 2016 VA examination report does not attribute the Veteran's symptoms to any source.  The JMR shows that it was agreed that the July 2019 and June 2022 VA negative opinions lack probative value.  Although another negative VA opinion was obtained in February 2024, the examiner failed to substantially comply with the Board's January 2024 remand.  That remand directed the examiner to explain the reasons for his or her conclusion.  However, the February 2024 examiner, a psychologist, merely summarized the medical evidence and the prior opinions of other health care providers, without providing her own rationale as to why the Veteran's PTSD has not resulted in the need for aid and attendance.  E.g., "The PTSD has not been noted to be the reason for the housebound or bedridden," and "It has been indicated that it is due to physical conditions" (emphasis added).  This opinion therefore lacks probative value.  Neives-Rodriguez v. Peake, 22 Vet. App. 295, 304 (2008).  

Service connection is in effect for PTSD, evaluated as 100 percent disabling under 38 C.F.R. § 4.130, Diagnostic Code (DC) 9411.  As provided for under DC 9411, the Veteran's symptoms are shown to include gross impairment in communication, and an intermittent inability to perform activities of daily living, including maintenance of minimal personal hygiene.  In Mittleider v. West, 11 Vet. App. 181 (1998), the Court of Veterans Appeals (Court) found that when it is not possible to separate the effects of the service-connected disability from a nonservice-connected condition, 38 C.F.R. § 3.102, which requires the Board to employ reasonable doubt, dictates that such signs and symptoms be attributed to the service-connected disability.  Given the lack of probative value of the VA opinions, there is an insufficient basis to dissociate the Veteran's PTSD symptoms from the residuals of his stroke.  The evidence shows that his symptoms include a daily need for medication management. This raises a reasonable doubt as to whether the Veteran requires care or assistance on a regular basis to protect him from the hazards or dangers incident to his daily environment.  Id.  The Board therefore finds that the evidence is sufficient to show that the Veteran is so helpless as a result of service-connected disability that he is in need of the regular aid and attendance of another person due to service-connected disability.  38 C.F.R. § 3.352.   

(Continued on next page) 

The grant of special monthly compensation based on the need for regular aid and attendance effectively renders moot any issue of entitlement to special monthly compensation on the basis of being housebound, since special monthly compensation based on aid and attendance is the higher benefit and payable at a higher rate.  

 

 

MATTHEW W. BLACKWELDER

Veterans Law Judge

Board of Veterans' Appeals

Attorney for the Board	T.S.E., Counsel

The Board's decision in this case is binding only with respect to the instant matter decided. This decision is not precedential and does not establish VA policies or interpretations of general applicability. 38 C.F.R. § 20.1303.
